spain-italy-border-checks.headline: Spain reinstates border checks on arrivals from Italy in tit-for-tat move
spain-italy-border-checks.body_md:
Spain began checking passports and visas on travellers arriving from Italy at midnight on Saturday, matching a move Rome made a week earlier — and turning a bilateral migration dispute into the most serious test of Schengen's border-free promise in years.

The checks, which Madrid says will run until 7 September, apply at Spanish ports and airports and target identity and nationality verification; non-EU nationals may also be asked to show a valid visa or residence permit. Spain's interior ministry framed the move as a response to "persistent irregular migration pressure" — official language for a straightforward retaliation against Italy's own suspension of free movement with Spain, imposed on 31 July.

## From Ceuta to reciprocity

The root of the dispute lies on Spain's North African coast. On 30–31 July, an estimated 72,000 people crossed from Morocco into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta in one of the largest single migration surges the EU's external border has recorded, exploiting the confusion after a Spanish court ruling on the legal status of swimmers reaching the territory by sea. Spanish authorities said 80 people died in the crossing; Moroccan human-rights monitors put the toll higher, at 141 and rising. Some 70,000 of those who entered were subsequently returned to Morocco, but hundreds of unaccompanied children remain in overstretched Spanish reception facilities.

![The Ceuta border fence separating Spain's North African enclave from Morocco](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/2/21/Ceuta_border_fence.jpg)

Italy's government cited the risk of secondary movement — migrants who land in Spain travelling on to Italy — in ordering a one-month suspension of Schengen free movement with Madrid, covering air and sea arrivals since the two countries share no land border. Deputy Prime Minister Antonio Tajani called it "a necessary choice to safeguard the security of our citizens," and Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni's office has said Rome will not revisit the decision before 15 August.

Spain has rejected the justification outright. Foreign Minister José Manuel Albares described Italy's checks as "a torpedo fired at the hull of European unity," and Madrid has demanded Rome treat Spanish citizens the same as other EU nationals or face reciprocal measures — a threat it has now made good on.

## A wider crack

What began as a dispute over one crossing has exposed how quickly the Schengen area's national-security exemptions can be invoked between two of its largest members. Finland, the Netherlands, Denmark, the Czech Republic and Sweden have shown sympathy for Italy's position, while France has independently tightened its own checks on arrivals from Spain — suggesting the Ceuta shock is rippling well beyond the two capitals directly involved. The European Commission has said existing Schengen provisions already cover emergencies like Ceuta, implicitly questioning the need for either country's unilateral action.

With both sets of checks currently timed to expire in the first half of September, the immediate question is whether either government blinks first — or whether the dispute hardens into a longer-term precedent for suspending free movement whenever migration pressure spikes at Europe's periphery.

reform-uk-poll-lead-narrows.headline: Reform UK's poll lead narrows to within margin of error
reform-uk-poll-lead-narrows.body_md:
Three weeks ago, Reform UK's lead over Labour was the defining fact of British politics — wide enough that Westminster had stopped debating whether Nigel Farage could become prime minister and started debating when. That gap has all but closed. The latest YouGov voting intention poll, conducted 2–3 August for The Times and Sky News, puts Reform on 23% and Labour on 22% — a one-point margin that sits inside the poll's margin of error. YouGov's own tracker notes it has now been three weeks since Reform last posted a lead that cleared that statistical bar.

Reform remains, on most counts, the largest single party. Its support across pollsters this year has ranged from the low twenties up to 28% at its spring peak, when Labour was mired in the low twenties under Keir Starmer. PollCheck's seven-poll moving average, updated 6 August, has Reform at 23.6% — but now trailing Labour on 25.4%, a reversal that would have seemed unthinkable in May.

## What changed

The hinge point was 20 July, when Andy Burnham succeeded Starmer as Labour leader and prime minister after accepting King Charles's invitation to form a government. The switch delivered an immediate polling bounce: within a week, More in Common had Labour ahead 28% to 24%, and YouGov had the two parties level at 22%. Ipsos found Burnham preferred as prime minister over both Farage and Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch, and by late July, 48% of adults said they wanted a Burnham-led Labour government at the next election against 29% for a Farage-led Reform — a far wider gap than the voting-intention numbers alone suggest, implying Reform's support is broader than it is deep.

Reform's own troubles compounded the squeeze. Farage has spent August contesting a Sunday Times report that he received an undeclared £5m personal gift from cryptocurrency billionaire Christopher Harborne, on top of some £25m in party funding from the same donor — a disclosure that triggered Farage's resignation as MP for Clacton and a subsequent byelection. He has called the reporting an "establishment hit job" and is weighing legal action, while the government moves to tighten donation-disclosure rules via the Representation of the People Bill. Pollster Sir John Curtice and elections expert Lord Hayward have both said the cross-poll trend now points to genuine decline rather than noise, prompting a public dispute between Farage and YouGov over the tracker's reliability.

## Why traders are watching

A Reform majority was the scenario UK-focused desks had been pricing tail risk against — sweeping deregulation, a harder line on immigration and trade, and open questions over Bank of England independence. A polling race this close cuts that probability meaningfully, which is one reason gilt yields and sterling positioning have become more sensitive to Burnham's own missteps than to Farage's. The next real test of durability comes with September's party conference season and the following YouGov tracker; a fourth or fifth consecutive poll inside the margin of error would confirm this is a trend rather than a blip.

royal-navy-russian-vessels.headline: Royal Navy spends 25% more time monitoring Russian vessels in UK waters
royal-navy-russian-vessels.body_md:
The Royal Navy spent 25% more time this year shadowing Russian warships near British waters than it did over the same period in 2025, according to figures released by the Ministry of Defence this week — the clearest sign yet that London views Russia's maritime activity as a persistent, low-grade threat rather than an occasional nuisance.

In July alone, Royal Navy assets spent 21 days tracking two Russian frigates, the Neustrashimy and the Admiral Grigorovich, as they escorted tankers belonging to Moscow's so-called shadow fleet through the Channel and North Sea. Offshore patrol vessels HMS Tyne, HMS Mersey and HMS Severn took turns on the tasking, backed by Wildcat helicopters from 815 Naval Air Squadron and Merlin submarine-hunters from 814 Squadron. On 20 July, the Neustrashimy fired its guns — 20 rounds from its 100mm mount and 30 from a 30mm battery — in international waters off the UK and French coasts, a live-fire drill the MoD logged rather than escalated.

![HMS Somerset, a Royal Navy Type 23 frigate, similar to those tasked with shadowing Russian vessels](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/f/f0/Royal_Navy_Type_23_Frigate_HMS_Somerset_MOD_45153155.jpg)

## Escort duty for an evasion network

The frigates' job is less about projecting Russian naval power than protecting it — specifically the ageing, opaquely-owned tankers that move sanctioned oil around the price cap imposed after the invasion of Ukraine. The UK has now sanctioned more than 500 vessels linked to the shadow fleet, part of a squeeze that contributed to a 24% year-on-year fall in Russian oil and gas revenue in 2025. An estimated 300 shadow fleet vessels passed through or near UK waters in the first quarter of this year alone.

But sanctions on paper have not translated cleanly into enforcement at sea. Since March, when Downing Street authorised the armed forces to board sanctioned ships in UK waters, at least 94 shadow fleet transits went unchallenged before the Royal Marines and National Crime Agency finally boarded the tanker Smyrtos in the Channel on 14 June — the first such interdiction. Commander Matt Millyard of HMS Somerset, which logged over 24,000 nautical miles on Russia-watching duties this year, called the mission "exactly what the Royal Navy exists to do, protect the UK and our allies"; critics in Parliament have been less charitable about the gap between presence and interdiction.

## Cables, not just convoys

The deeper worry animating the extra sea-days is not the tankers but what else Russian vessels might be doing near them. The intelligence-gathering ship Yantar was tracked off Scotland in November loitering near undersea cable routes, prompting a new joint patrol arrangement with Norway to guard North Atlantic infrastructure. Germany separately said in the past year that several of its warships had been sabotaged, and NATO officials increasingly describe Baltic and North Sea infrastructure — cables, pipelines, wind farms — as a live target set, not a hypothetical one.

None of this marks a break from the pattern set since 2022: Western navies have been leaning into Russian-shadowing duties for four years, and the trend line, not any single incident, is the story. The MoD reshuffled its own leadership on this brief in June, when Dan Jarvis replaced John Healey as defence secretary after a budget dispute — a change worth watching as the department weighs whether stepped-up monitoring can be matched by the political will, and hulls, to actually stop the ships it is watching.

israel-archaeology-west-bank.headline: Israel accused of 'weaponising archaeology' at West Bank heritage sites
israel-archaeology-west-bank.body_md:
The dig sits inside a Palestinian town, but the signage, the funding and the security perimeter around it are Israeli. At Sebastia, a hilltop of Roman columns and Ottoman stonework north of Nablus, archaeologists working for Israel's Civil Administration have spent the past 15 months excavating what officials call the Shomron National Park — and Palestinian residents call the slow annexation of their land.

A BBC investigation, reported by Sebastian Usher and Callum Tulley, examined how digs at Sebastia and at Herodium, King Herod's fortress-palace near Bethlehem, have become instruments in Israel's territorial claim over the occupied West Bank. The reporters found that archaeological designation is now routinely followed by expropriation orders: roughly 450 acres around Sebastia and about 80 acres at Herodium have been earmarked for seizure, according to Civil Administration filings reviewed by the BBC and by the Israeli monitoring group Peace Now.

![Columned Roman street among the ruins at Sebastia in the occupied West Bank](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/5/58/Columned_street_-_panoramio.jpg)

## A biblical capital, a modern land dispute

Sebastia's ruins span three millennia — Iron Age fortifications from when the hill was Samaria, capital of the northern Israelite kingdom in the ninth century BCE, layered under a Roman forum, a Crusader hall and a mosque built into the remains of a Byzantine church. Israel's Heritage Ministry has allocated 113 million shekels (£27.8m) to develop West Bank archaeological sites this year, with 32 million shekels earmarked for Sebastia alone, restoring a colonnaded street, building a new access road and constructing paid-entry visitor facilities.

For Abu Mudif, a local landowner, the excavation has meant losing olive groves his family has worked for generations. "It is like having your soul ripped away," he told the BBC. "I cannot imagine myself without my land." Mohammed Azem, the village mayor, and Nahed Sakha, a restaurant owner facing a demolition order for his premises near the ruins, describe a town increasingly cut off from the acropolis it grew up around — the archaeological zone falls in Area C, under full Israeli control, while the modern town sits in Area B.

## Scholarship as leverage

Alon Arad, director of the Israeli civil-society group Emek Shaveh, which tracks archaeology's political uses in the occupied territories, put the mechanism plainly: "You use archaeology to excavate and rewrite narrative, but also to reallocate lands from Palestinian to Israeli." Palestinian officials make the same charge from the other direction, accusing Israel of foregrounding Jewish-era finds at Sebastia while downplaying the site's Roman, Crusader and Islamic layers.

Israel rejects the framing entirely. UNESCO's decision in July to add Sebastia to the World Heritage List — and simultaneously to its List of World Heritage in Danger, a designation reserved for sites under acute threat — passed over Israeli objections. Foreign Minister Gideon Saar dismissed the vote as a Palestinian attempt to erase Jewish history: "No vote in an international organisation can change history."

The dispute now sits with two authorities that rarely move fast. UNESCO's in-danger listing carries no enforcement power beyond diplomatic pressure, and Israel's Civil Administration has continued issuing expropriation orders at Sebastia through this year, most recently in February. Watch for whether that pace holds through the annual UNESCO monitoring report, and for whether the Shomron National Park's paid-entry infrastructure — due for further construction this year — becomes the fact on the ground that outlasts the argument over who gets to write the history beneath it.

oklo-leadership-overhaul.headline: Oklo leadership overhaul raises questions as small-reactor commercialisation nears
oklo-leadership-overhaul.body_md:
Oklo, the nuclear-fuel and small-reactor startup racing to put America's first commercial fast reactor on the grid, has spent the past four months reshuping its top ranks — a board expansion, a chief technology officer moved sideways, and five long-serving executives newly formalised as officers. None of it looks like a company in crisis. All of it lands at an unusually pointed moment: construction is underway on the reactor Oklo needs to actually start making money.

On April 8, chief technology officer Pat Schweiger agreed to step back into a "senior technical advisor" role, a mutual arrangement the company says lets it keep drawing on his expertise while someone else runs engineering day to day. Two days later the board grew from seven directors to eleven, adding Mark Peters (president of MITRE), former Dominion Energy executive David Christian, Shopify operations VP Derek Kan and Standard Lithium chief executive David Park, while Michael Thompson took the newly created role of lead independent director. Then, on July 22, the board formally elevated five existing staffers — product chief Alexandra Renner, chief of staff John Hanson, general counsel Vivek Narayanadas, engineering SVP Erik Lassen and controller Michael Dixon — to executive-officer status, with no new pay or equity attached.

## A pivot, not a purge

What's notable is who *isn't* on that list of departures: nobody senior appears to have quit or been pushed out, and no severance or dispute language shows up in the filings. That argues against reading this as strategy misalignment at the top. It reads more like a company converting from an engineering-and-permitting outfit into one that has to build, staff and eventually operate a licensed nuclear facility — a different set of skills, and a bigger bench, than getting a design through the Nuclear Regulatory Commission. The company's own framing — "to support its continued growth" — is boilerplate, but the timing tracks: this is the year Oklo actually started pouring concrete.

![Oklo co-founder Jacob DeWitte (left), now the company's board chairman, at CES 2026](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/9/9f/CES_2026_-_Jacob_DeWitte%2C_JoeBen_Bevirt%2C_JP_Nauseef_01.jpg)

## The commercialisation math

Excavation is nearly finished at the first Aurora powerhouse site at Idaho National Laboratory, and the Department of Energy has signed off on a preliminary safety analysis — real regulatory progress toward the late-2027/2028 commercial-operation target. In early August, Oklo's separate Groves isotope test reactor reached first criticality just eleven months after groundbreaking, which the company calls the fastest such transition for any privately funded full-scale reactor.

The balance sheet tells the other half of the story. Second-quarter revenue of $1.2 million beat the $83,800 analysts had modelled, but the operating loss reached $124.2 million year-to-date, and Oklo raised its 2026 cash-burn guidance to $120–150 million and capital-spending guidance to $400–500 million — both up sharply as construction accelerates. TipRanks holds a Neutral rating on the stock, and the average analyst price target has slipped from roughly $112 to $89 as the capital intensity of actually building reactors sets in against the earlier hype.

The next real test isn't another board announcement — it's whether Aurora-INL construction stays on schedule through 2027, and whether Oklo's newly formalised operations team can hold the line on that budget once concrete gives way to commissioning.

water-utility-cyberattacks-seven-states.headline: Cyberattacks hit water facilities in seven US states
water-utility-cyberattacks-seven-states.body_md:
The Federal Bureau of Investigation is treating it as one campaign, not seven unrelated break-ins. Since July 27, water and wastewater utilities in at least seven states — Minnesota, Michigan, Georgia, New Jersey, South Dakota and others — have reported hackers gaining remote access to the industrial equipment that runs their plants. By the following week, federal officials said the number had grown to at least twelve states. Nobody has been publicly named as responsible, but multiple US intelligence sources point to Iran.

No one has gotten sick. The Minnesota Bureau of Criminal Apprehension and Michigan's environmental agency both say no drinking water has been contaminated, and operators caught the intrusions before anything worse happened. But the attacks did what they needed to do: they knocked operators out of the systems that watch pressure, chlorine levels and pump flow, forcing plants back onto manual controls that most modern utilities haven't relied on in decades.

## Thirty plants, one weekend

The clearest picture comes from Minnesota, where more than 30 municipal water systems were hit over the weekend of July 26–27. Attackers got into the plants' programmable logic controllers — the small industrial computers, often made by Rockwell Automation, that physically open and close valves and turn pumps on and off — and then changed the IP addresses and passwords protecting them. That's a specific, low-tech lockout: it doesn't require breaching a corporate network or stealing credentials through phishing. It just requires the controller to be reachable from the open internet in the first place, which a large share of small water systems still are.

![Chart recorders on an industrial control panel of the kind used to monitor water treatment operations](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/b/b3/Chart_recorders_of_a_control_panel.JPG)

CISA's acting director, Nick Andersen, said the agency is "observing a significant increase in cyber threat actors targeting programmable logic controllers at water utilities," adding that the activity "has resulted in boil water notices and sustained manual operations" at some sites. Georgia and Michigan confirmed similar intrusions days later; Michigan's environment department said nine communities reported activity matching the federal warning, though all systems "continued to operate safely."

## A familiar signature

The pattern isn't new — it's an escalation of one the water sector has seen before. In November 2023, a group calling itself CyberAv3ngers broke into a booster station at the Municipal Water Authority of Aliquippa, Pennsylvania, by exploiting a Unitronics controller that was still running its factory-default password. The US Treasury later sanctioned CyberAv3ngers as a front for Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps Cyber-Electronic Command. This summer's attacks look like the same playbook run at scale: instead of one controller with a default password, investigators say the intrusions this time exploited a known authentication-bypass flaw in Rockwell Automation Logix controllers, a vulnerability rated 9.8 out of 10 for severity that utilities were supposed to have patched years ago.

That gap — a fix that existed but wasn't applied — is the part that has regulators most frustrated. Water utilities are a famously fragmented sector: roughly 50,000 community water systems across the country, most of them small, publicly owned, and running on budgets that leave little room for a dedicated cybersecurity staffer. CISA has said its scanning still finds water-system control equipment exposed directly to the internet even after months of public warnings.

## Regulators scramble to catch up

The response has moved fast for Washington. The EPA, which shares oversight of drinking-water cybersecurity with CISA and the FBI, has pushed out roughly $9 million in fresh grants aimed at midsize and large systems, on top of earlier funding for rural utilities through the Rural Community Assistance Partnership. In the Senate, the Water Resources Development Act of 2026 carries new cybersecurity provisions and would reauthorize a resilience program for midsize and large drinking-water systems, while a separate bipartisan bill from Senators John Boozman and Mark Kelly — the FLOWS Act — would create a targeted grant program for small and rural utilities to modernize aging, internet-exposed controls. The American Water Works Association has backed both efforts, arguing that voluntary guidance has run its course and that funding, not just advisories, is what closes the gap between a known vulnerability and a patched one.

For an industry that has largely escaped the kind of binding cybersecurity mandates already imposed on the electric grid, the timing matters. Water utilities remain governed mostly by state-level rules and EPA sanitary surveys rather than a single federal cybersecurity standard, and insurers who cover municipal utilities have been watching the sector's exposure grow for years without a comparable pricing framework to the one that emerged after repeated grid-focused incidents.

What happens next depends on two things moving in parallel: whether US officials formally attribute the campaign to Iran, which would trigger a different diplomatic and possibly military calculus than a criminal ransomware case, and whether the Senate moves the water-resources bill before the current legislative session runs out. CISA has said it will keep publishing which controller models and configurations are being targeted, giving the clearest real-time signal of whether the campaign is still expanding.

central-europe-heatwave-nuclear.headline: Central Europe heatwave sets records as Danube hits record lows and a nuclear plant throttles back
central-europe-heatwave-nuclear.body_md:
Slovakia's national weather service confirmed on Thursday that a village in the country's south, Dolné Plachtince, had reached 42.2°C — a new all-time national record, and the second time in as many days the mark had been broken. A day earlier, Austria recorded 41.2°C at Bad Deutsch-Altenburg. In Budapest, the thermometer never fell below 28°C overnight, the warmest night the Hungarian capital has logged since records began.

The numbers are striking on their own. What makes this heatwave a story for energy markets rather than just the weather page is what has happened to the Danube. The river that cools Central Europe's nuclear fleet has fallen to levels not seen in decades, and the region's power system is now absorbing the consequences in real time.

## A river too thin to cool a reactor

Nuclear plants along the Danube don't just need electricity to run — they need a reliable flow of river water to carry away waste heat from the reactor core. Regulators cap how warm that water can be when it's returned to the river, to protect fish and other aquatic life downstream. When the river itself is low and already warm from weeks of heat, plants run out of headroom on both sides of that equation: less water to draw, and less capacity to cool it before it goes back in.

Hungary's Paks plant, 100km south of Budapest on the Danube's bank, has taken the hardest hit. Paks normally supplies close to half of Hungary's electricity from its four reactors. Officials confirmed this week it has been running at roughly 10% of capacity, after water levels at the Budapest gauge fell to around 23 centimetres — well below the previous record low of 33 centimetres set in 2018.

![The Hungarian Parliament building on the banks of the Danube in Budapest](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/3/30/Hungarian_Parliament_Building%2C_Budapest.jpg)

Slovakia's own nuclear station, which draws on the same river system, is faring better but is still constrained, running at around 80% of rated output. Romania's Cernavodă plant came closer to a full shutdown: engineers there sank barges loaded with rock into the river to redirect flow toward the plant's intake after the Danube's discharge fell to roughly a third of its long-term July average — a scramble that, for now, has kept a second reactor online.

## The market is already pricing it in

The timing compounds the problem. This is peak air-conditioning season, when demand for power is highest and the room for error in supply is thinnest. Utilities across the region have been forced to lean harder on gas-fired plants and cross-border imports to fill the gap left by derated nuclear capacity, and other thermal generators are hitting the same river-cooling limits — French nuclear output has been cut by roughly 11% amid its own heat-driven reactor derating, with EDF trimming output at Blayais and extending an outage at Gravelines.

The price effect is already visible. Electricity bills in Germany and France rose by an estimated €700 million combined during a June heat spell, well before this month's records were set, and Italian spot prices have pushed toward €500 per megawatt-hour. Every megawatt of nuclear output lost to the heat has to be replaced by something, and in a market still absorbing elevated gas prices tied to the Strait of Hormuz standoff, that something is rarely cheap. The mechanics are straightforward: gas-fired plants tend to set the marginal price in European power markets, so as they're called on more often to cover for constrained nuclear and hydro capacity, wholesale electricity prices ratchet up in step with gas.

## What happens if the heat doesn't break

Europe has been here before, though not quite this badly. The 2018 and 2022 droughts also forced river-cooled reactors offline and pushed up power prices, and in both cases the disruption eased once autumn rain returned. What's different this time is the starting point: this heatwave arrives on top of a dry spring, meaning reservoirs and groundwater had less of a cushion to begin with, and Slovakia has now broken its national temperature record twice within six weeks.

Operators are managing rather than resolving the constraint. Hungary has room to raise the permitted discharge temperature at Paks in a supply emergency, with ministerial sign-off, and Romania's barge-and-rock intervention buys time rather than capacity. None of it adds new cooling water to the system — it only rearranges how the shortage is shared.

The next inflection point is meteorological, not regulatory: forecasters are watching for the first sustained rainfall over the Alpine and Carpathian catchments that feed the Danube, which would be the clearest signal that river levels — and with them, reactor output — are on the way back up. Until then, the region's grid operators are effectively trading hydrology for gas, one degree of river temperature at a time.

france-wildfire-arrests.headline: France records 420 arrests as wildfire season intensifies
france-wildfire-arrests.body_md:
French police have arrested more than 420 people this fire season on suspicion of setting or carelessly starting blazes that have now torn through over 117,000 hectares of French countryside — an area larger than greater London. The figure, updated this week by the interior ministry, has climbed steadily since Laurent Nuñez, the interior minister, first disclosed 184 arrests in late July. By last weekend it had passed 400. Among those held, well over a hundred are minors.

The arrests are the clearest sign yet that France's escalating wildfire crisis is not simply a story about heat and drought. According to the interior ministry, roughly nine in ten of the more than 14,000 fire outbreaks recorded since the season began were started by human activity — carelessness with machinery, discarded cigarettes, campfires — and investigators believe about a third of those were deliberate. That distinction matters: it reframes a summer of fire less as an act of nature and more as a matter of enforcement, land management and, increasingly, criminal investigation.

![A Canadair water bomber fights a wildfire near Toulon, in the Var — the department at the centre of this year's longest-running blaze](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/1/15/Canadair_water_bomber_fighting_a_fire_outside_Toulon_-a.jpg)

## A season without precedent in the Var

The department bearing the brunt is the Var, on the Mediterranean coast east of Marseille, where a fire in the Gros Bessillon area has burned for more than a fortnight — what Nuñez called "the longest wildfire ever recorded in the Var." At its peak the blaze forced the evacuation of roughly 2,500 people and drew 1,250 firefighters, backed by Canadair water bombers, Dash aircraft and helicopters. Fires that broke out earlier in the season in Gironde, near Bordeaux, and in Aude have since been brought under control, but the Var's mix of dense pine forest, steep terrain and repeated mistral winds has kept crews on the ground since late July.

![A Canadair CL-415 drops seawater over a wildfire in the smoke-filled hills near Villeneuve-Loubet](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/b/b4/Aerial_firefighting_in_Villeneuve-Loubet_%281%29.jpg)

France's 2026 season is already among its worst on record, exceeded in scale only by 1949, when a series of fires in the Landes killed 82 people. This year's toll on people has been lower — French officials have not attributed direct fire deaths to the current outbreaks — but the area burned, at well over 100,000 hectares nationally, rivals the historic benchmark. Spain has fared worse still, with more than 220,000 hectares burned, making this summer's combined Iberian and French losses among the largest Europe has recorded in a single season.

## Enforcement as the policy response

What distinguishes this year is the scale of the criminal response layered on top of the firefighting effort. Arrests have run well ahead of prior seasons: 32 suspects detained in a single sweep across 22 departments in mid-July, doubling to over 300 by month's end, and now beyond 420. Nuñez has framed the arrests as evidence that French authorities are treating arson and reckless fire-starting as a security priority rather than an unfortunate side effect of a hot, dry summer — internal security forces, not just fire brigades, are now central to the response.

That framing carries an implicit admission: if roughly a third of ignitions are deliberate and nine in ten are human in origin, then reducing outbreaks depends as much on policing, prosecution and public behaviour as on rainfall. It is a harder problem to solve than weather, and one without an obvious ceiling — arrests can rise each week the season continues, as they have done since June.

## The economic tail

The insurance and reconstruction implications are becoming a story of their own. Analysts estimate France's wildfire losses this year could reach €10–15 billion, with insured losses running into the billions of euros — potentially the country's costliest wildfire season on record. Unlike floods and droughts, wildfire damage in France sits outside the state-backed natural catastrophe compensation scheme, so private insurers are expected to absorb most of the recovery bill; some have already begun covering hotel costs for evacuated policyholders. Restoration spending across the five hardest-hit eurozone countries is estimated at €3.1 billion so far this year, a figure that does not yet include the slower-moving costs to homes, tourism and agriculture.

The longer-run risk map is shifting too. A July analysis by AXA's climate research unit found that the average number of high-wildfire-risk days around French cities could rise by nearly 70% by 2050, and by close to 130% by century's end, as fire-prone conditions spread beyond the traditional Mediterranean hotspots into central and northern France. Combined with a record-arrest season concentrated in the south, the pattern being described by officials and insurers alike is structural rather than cyclical: not a single bad summer, but a widening zone of risk that reconstruction planning, agricultural insurance and regional infrastructure will need to price in going forward.

## What comes next

The Var fire's perimeter is largely secured but not yet declared over, and forecasters are watching for another round of mistral winds that could reignite hotspots, as happened in early August. The interior ministry has signalled it will continue to publish arrest tallies through the end of the season, which typically runs into September in southern France — meaning the 420 figure is very unlikely to be the final count. Separately, the scale of insured losses will start to firm up as adjusters complete assessments this autumn, a number that will matter well beyond France's borders for how European insurers price wildfire risk next year.

fda-mrna-flu-narcolepsy-approvals.headline: FDA approves first mRNA flu vaccine and new narcolepsy drug
fda-mrna-flu-narcolepsy-approvals.body_md:
Three unrelated approvals landed at the Food and Drug Administration within a 24-hour window this week — a vaccine, a sleep drug and a cancer therapy, each validating a different corner of biotech that has spent years promising more than it delivered. None of the three companies involved coordinated the timing. That they arrived together says more about the FDA's approval calendar than about any shared scientific thread.

## The vaccine that took two tries

Moderna's mFLUSIVA, cleared on August 5th, is the first mRNA-based influenza vaccine approved anywhere in the world — a notable extension of the platform that produced the company's COVID-19 shot into a market it has chased for years. The approval covers adults 50 and older outright; for those 65 and up, clearance came via the accelerated pathway, contingent on a postmarketing study, after the FDA initially refused to even review Moderna's application in February. The dispute was narrow but consequential: the agency's then-vaccine chief objected to Moderna benchmarking mFLUSIVA against a standard-dose comparator in older adults rather than the high-dose shot the FDA recommends for that group. Moderna resubmitted with the population split into two age-based tracks, and the review restarted.[^1] In trials, the vaccine was reported to be roughly 27% more effective than a standard flu shot — though whether that translates to real-world uptake is unproven, and analysts are not treating the approval as an immediate windfall. Moderna shares actually fell about 1.5% on the news; Jefferies kept a Hold rating and a $45 price target, arguing meaningful flu revenue is unlikely before 2027.[^2]

![FDA headquarters entrance, White Oak campus, Silver Spring, Maryland](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/3/33/FDA_Sign_%26_Bldg_21_at_Entrance_%285204602349%29.jpg)

## A sleep disorder's root cause, and a virus that hunts tumors

A day earlier, the FDA approved Takeda's Orzeyful (oveporexton) for narcolepsy type 1 in adults — the first drug designed to address the disease's underlying mechanism, a deficiency of the brain signalling molecule orexin, rather than just its symptoms. Across two 12-week placebo-controlled trials totalling 273 patients, the twice-daily tablet improved wakefulness and cut cataplexy episodes, sleep paralysis and hallucinations.[^3] Takeda estimates roughly 120,000 people in the US live with narcolepsy type 1, a small population that explains the company's own guidance that the approval won't materially move its fiscal 2026-27 earnings — shares rose only about 1.4%. One caveat worth flagging for anyone pricing in a near-term launch: Orzeyful's scheduling under the Controlled Substances Act is still pending a decision from the Drug Enforcement Administration, which could delay availability.[^4]

The third approval, granted August 6th to Replimune's Tudriqev (vusolimogene oderparepvec-wtpg) in combination with Bristol Myers Squibb's nivolumab, treats advanced melanoma that has progressed despite prior anti-PD-1 therapy. It works by a genetically modified herpes simplex virus engineered to replicate inside and destroy tumor cells — an approach known as oncolytic viral therapy that has circled clinical relevance for over a decade without a major US approval. This was Replimune's third attempt at the FDA after two prior rejections, in July 2025 and April 2026. The supporting trial enrolled 140 patients with 91 evaluable; 24% achieved an objective response, lasting a median of nearly 14 months.[^5] Replimune shares rose more than 8% intraday to $12.86 before slipping in after-hours and premarket trading — a reminder that accelerated approval, granted on a surrogate endpoint, still leaves the company on the hook for a confirmatory trial to prove real clinical benefit. Two sell-side desks, Leerink and Wedbush, upgraded the stock regardless, with Leerink lifting its target to $17 from $11.[^6]

What ties the three together, if anything, is that each represents a first-of-kind clearance for a platform technology — mRNA vaccines beyond pandemic use, orexin-targeted neurology, and engineered oncolytic viruses — rather than an incremental label expansion. The next test for all three is commercial, not regulatory: Moderna's flu vaccine faces its first real readout during the fall season now underway, the DEA's scheduling decision will determine when Orzeyful actually reaches patients, and Replimune's confirmatory melanoma trial will decide whether Tudriqev's accelerated approval converts to full approval or gets withdrawn.

harrogate-army-college-abuse-allegations.headline: Streeting 'sickened' by sex abuse allegations at Army's Harrogate college
harrogate-army-college-abuse-allegations.body_md:
Four women have told the BBC they were raped or sexually assaulted as teenage recruits at the Army Foundation College in Harrogate, the sole training establishment for 16- and 17-year-olds joining the British Army — and the account has pulled a response from the very top of the Ministry of Defence.

Defence Secretary Wes Streeting called the reports "absolutely sickened," adding that "my heart goes out to this courageous woman who's spoken up, having been so badly failed." Speaking to reporters on 7 August during a visit to the Babcock shipyard in Rosyth, he said the department owed recruits "the very highest standards in uniform" and that he needed to "assure myself that we're doing everything we can to deliver the culture change that's needed."

The women's accounts, spanning roughly five years at the college, describe a pattern rather than a single incident. One, given the pseudonym Tilly, said she was raped at 17 by a fellow soldier after being invited into his room, an assault she said lasted hours. Another, Monica, alleged she was trapped in a room and sexually assaulted. A third, Amy, said harassment was severe enough that she slept across her bedroom door because the lock was broken and she feared men entering. A fourth, Ellie, alleged instructors rated female recruits' appearances aloud and walked into women's dormitories unannounced while cadets were undressed.

![Defence Secretary Wes Streeting, whose department oversees the Army Foundation College](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/5/5d/Official_portrait_of_Wes_Streeting_MP_crop_2.jpg)

## The numbers behind the accounts

North Yorkshire Police received 16 reports of sexual offences linked to the college in the year to June, spanning exposure, voyeurism and sexual assault, with three now under active investigation. The MoD's own figures are starker still: 176 complaints of inappropriate sexual behaviour at the college between January 2018 and June 2025, including 32 against permanent staff and 144 against junior soldiers themselves. Between 2021 and 2024 alone, the department logged 122 investigations into sexual offences against under-18s at the college, 80 of them involving sexual assault.

The college is not new to this scrutiny. Instructors there were court-martialled in 2017 and 2018 over alleged abuse of recruits, and a separate MoD-commissioned inquiry into conduct at the site between 2014 and 2018 was later shelved. What's changed is the volume of fresh allegations reaching police in a single year, and a defence secretary willing to put his name to a public apology rather than a written statement.

Harrogate's MP, Tom Gordon, has written to Streeting demanding an independent inquiry into culture and safeguarding at the college, a call echoed by Emma Lewell, a Labour member of the Commons Defence Committee, who has questioned whether the college should keep operating in its current form. About 1,300 recruits pass through the college's Phase 1 training at any one time, some as young as 16 — the youngest cohort the Army takes in at all. Streeting has not yet said whether he will order an independent inquiry or rely on internal MoD review; that decision, and whatever North Yorkshire Police's three live investigations turn up, is the next thing worth watching.

trump-birthright-citizenship-renewed.headline: Trump renews push to restrict birthright citizenship
trump-birthright-citizenship-renewed.body_md:
President Trump has gone back to the birthright citizenship fight he lost at the Supreme Court five weeks ago — this time with a narrower target and a different legal theory.

On Thursday the president signed two executive orders reopening a battle that seemed settled on June 30, when the Supreme Court ruled 6–3 in *Trump v. Barbara* that his original attempt to strip citizenship from children born on US soil to undocumented or temporary immigrants was unconstitutional. Chief Justice John Roberts, writing for the majority, held that children born in the US to parents "unlawfully or temporarily present" are still "subject to the jurisdiction" of the United States and are citizens at birth under the 14th Amendment — the same reading the Court reached in 1898's *United States v. Wong Kim Ark*, the case that has anchored birthright citizenship for well over a century.

That first order, signed on Trump's first day back in office in January 2025, tried to deny automatic citizenship broadly to babies born to parents who were in the country illegally or on temporary visas. It never took effect; lower courts blocked it almost immediately, and the Supreme Court finished the job in June.

## A narrower wedge

The new pair of orders tries a different angle. One identifies specific categories of children the administration says fall outside constitutional protection — among them children of foreign government employees and of people classified as "alien enemies," including members of federally designated terrorist organizations. The White House frames this as consistent with, not opposed to, the *Barbara* ruling, pointing to narrow historical exceptions — diplomats' children, for instance — that the Court itself has long recognized. The second order directs the State Department and Department of Homeland Security to crack down on so-called birth tourism, which a White House fact sheet describes as people working with "malign syndicates" to enter the country and "exploit their temporary admission to obtain American citizenship." Neither order spells out a legal definition of birth tourism, and enforcement details are left to the two departments.

The administration is betting that a tighter, more surgical order will survive where a sweeping one failed — and that framing the categories as extensions of existing exceptions, rather than a rewrite of the 14th Amendment, gives it better odds in court.

Immigrant-rights groups are unconvinced. "The Supreme Court already decided this issue: birthright citizenship is guaranteed by the Constitution," said Cody Wofsy, deputy director of the ACLU's Immigrants' Rights Project, who argued *Barbara*. "No additional executive order can change the meaning of the Constitution. Any executive order that tries to rewrite birthright citizenship will meet the same fate as the last one."

The orders arrive alongside other citizenship-adjacent moves the White House touted this week, including 88 denaturalization cases filed against people it deems to have obtained citizenship improperly and tighter visa screening for 75 countries it classifies as high-risk.

Litigation is expected within days — the same coalition of ACLU affiliates, the Legal Defense Fund and immigrant-advocacy groups that won *Barbara* is the likely plaintiff again. Whether a federal judge grants an early injunction, as happened within weeks of the 2025 order, will be the first signal of how much runway this narrower version gets before it lands back in front of the same Supreme Court that just ruled against its predecessor.

conservatives-social-housing-ban.headline: Conservatives pledge to ban foreign nationals from social housing
conservatives-social-housing-ban.body_md:
The Conservative Party has unveiled a pledge to strip foreign nationals of access to social housing in England, promising that if elected the party would free up nearly a quarter of a million homes for British citizens by evicting non-EU tenants within six months of taking power.

The policy, announced this week by Shadow Work and Pensions Secretary Helen Whately, would bar anyone without British, Irish or EU citizenship from signing a new social tenancy, and would revoke the tenancies of those who already hold one. Couples in which one partner holds British, Irish or EU citizenship — including EU nationals with settled status — would remain eligible. A single tenant who holds none of those, the party says, would lose their home regardless of whether they have children.

> "Making Britain your home should be earned by working, paying tax and integrating," Whately said. "It should not come with a free ride on the benefits system."

Party leader Kemi Badenoch framed the announcement in blunter terms, vowing to end Britain's role as a "cash machine for the world." The Conservatives point to figures showing that 89% of lead social housing tenants in England were UK or Irish nationals in 2024–25 — a share the party wants at 100%, and one it says would liberate 228,144 homes for people further up council waiting lists.

![Kemi Badenoch, Conservative Party leader](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/d/d5/Official_portrait_of_Kemi_Badenoch_MP_crop_2%2C_2024.jpg)

## A crowded field on the right

The timing is telling. Reform UK, which has led national polling for months, proposed a similar ban earlier this year, and its response to the Tory announcement was pointed rather than welcoming. Shadow Home Secretary Zia Yusuf dismissed Badenoch's party as "shameless arsonist firefighters," arguing the plan doesn't go far enough because it still lets EU nationals with settled status keep their homes. "Under Reform," he said, "all social housing — old and new — will be for Brits." Nigel Farage was characteristically terser on social media: "The Tories copy every policy of ours."

Labour dismissed the proposal from the opposite direction, calling it "an unserious, unworkable proposal, copied from Reform, that does nothing to tackle the housing crisis." Housing charities were sharper still. Shelter chief executive Sarah Elliott said the plans "would brutally kick people out of their homes, including thousands of families and pensioners," while Kate Henderson of the National Housing Federation called evicting settled tenants "against our sector's values." The Chartered Institute of Housing flagged unresolved legal and operational questions, and the Royal College of Nursing warned that housing insecurity among migrant nursing staff could ripple into patient care.

## The labour-supply wrinkle

What the announcement does not address is where the workers go. Migrant labour is deeply embedded in exactly the sectors most reliant on lower-cost housing near their place of work: care, construction and hospitality. Health and Care Worker visa issuance has already fallen sharply — down from over 34,000 in one quarter of 2023 to around 2,000 a year later, as the last government tightened the route — and the construction industry says it is already short by more than 200,000 workers against a target of 225,000 new entrants by 2027. Hospitality has drawn more than one in ten of its workforce from arrivals since 2010.

None of that means social-housing tenants are the same people plugging those shortages — eligibility rules already exclude most migrants on temporary visas from social housing under the "no recourse to public funds" condition, a point Crisis chief executive Matt Downie made in response to the announcement. But the policy lands as a signal of direction rather than a costed plan: no timeline for implementation, no mechanism detailed for enforcement, and no assessment published of what tightening the wider immigration system further — a stated ambition alongside this pledge — would do to sectors already advertising for workers they cannot find.

## What's next

The Conservatives remain a distant third in national polling behind Labour and Reform, so this is a positioning exercise rather than imminent legislation. The next test is whether it holds up under scrutiny of the party's 2029 manifesto process, and whether Reform escalates with a still-tougher offer that pulls the debate further rightward before then.

burnham-prisoner-release-tour.headline: Burnham faces early test on prisoner releases as he launches cost-of-living tour
burnham-prisoner-release-tour.body_md:
Six weeks into the job, Andy Burnham has learned what every new prime minister eventually discovers: the small print of a policy can undo the headline. On 3 August his government confirmed that rapists and serious child sex offenders would be excluded from an early-release scheme designed to relieve England and Wales' overcrowded prisons. It was meant to draw a line under weeks of pressure. Instead it drew attention to who was left on the other side of it — including the two people convicted of killing PC Andrew Harper.

![Andy Burnham, UK Prime Minister](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/c/ca/Official_portrait_of_Andy_Burnham_MP_2026_%28cropped_3x4%29_2.jpg)

## A carve-out that satisfies no one

The scheme itself is a response to a genuine crunch: the prison population in England and Wales has passed 87,000 against a certified capacity of around 70,000, and the Public Accounts Committee warned earlier this year of "total gridlock" in the system. From October, most adults serving standard sentences will be released after a third of their term rather than 40% or 50%, cutting roughly 5,000 people's time inside over the scheme's first ten months.

Burnham's fix — excluding around 18,000 offenders convicted of rape, serious child sexual offences and grooming — was announced after a fortnight of mounting criticism. But manslaughter was not added to the exclusion list. Justice Secretary Alex Norris defended the line squarely: "These are decisions no Minister would ever want to take, but it is right these sickening crimes are excluded from these reforms." Extending the carve-out to manslaughter, officials argued, would gut the scheme's purpose of freeing up cells.

That left Jessie Cole and Albert Bowers — convicted of manslaughter over the 2019 death of PC Andrew Harper, who was dragged along a road by a car while attempting to stop a quad-bike theft — still eligible for release this autumn under standard terms. Harper's driver, Henry Long, sentenced separately and more severely, is unaffected. But the distinction between Long and his two accomplices has proven difficult to explain to a public that remembers the case as a single, brutal event.

Lissie Harper, the officer's widow, was blunt: "I am beyond appalled and bristling with anger to hear that Andrew's killers are soon to be free to roam the streets... This is an utter betrayal — and it's one I will not be able to forgive or forget." Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch called it a "partial climbdown" that had left victims facing "weeks of uncertainty and fear" while violent and domestic offenders still walk out in October. Burnham has not disputed the anger. "I fully understand the anger, anxiety and distress that's been caused," he said, promising "much tougher community measures" for offenders released early — a pledge long on tone, short on detail.

The episode matters less for its scale — a few thousand sentences shortened by months — than for what it says about a government still finding its footing. Burnham inherited the prisons crisis rather than created it, and the arithmetic behind the scheme is real. But the sequencing — announce, retreat under pressure, then defend a line that still leaves a household-name case exposed — is the kind of pattern that opposition parties learn to exploit and that erodes a leader's authority to make the next hard call.

## Listening, not yet answering

That vulnerability sits awkwardly alongside the other project Burnham launched this week: a nationwide "listening tour" on the cost of living, running through the rest of August and intended to feed into a ten-year plan for the economy. The format echoes the mayoral town-hall style that built his reputation in Greater Manchester, and the government is keen to point to concrete wins already delivered — a £2 cap on single bus fares outside London, modelled on Manchester's Bee Network, and a temporary cut in VAT on household electricity from 5% to zero, due to run from October and expected to trim about £45 off the average annual bill.

What the tour does not yet offer is anything new. No figures, no fresh commitments, just Burnham travelling to hear concerns he and his ministers have heard many times before. Framed as a "cost of living government," the exercise reads as much as reassurance-seeking as policymaking — an attempt to project engagement while the harder decisions, on prisons as much as on bills, are still being worked out in Whitehall.

The two stories share a thread. A prime minister only weeks into office is discovering that competence in opposition, or in city government, does not automatically translate into the discipline of national policy under scrutiny — where every exemption, every carve-out, invites the question of who was left off the list. The bus fare cap and the VAT cut are real, deliverable things; the manslaughter exclusion is a real, difficult gap. How Burnham handles the next version of this test — expected as more sentencing details firm up before the October start date — will say more about his premiership than either announcement alone.

union-obr-review-call.headline: Union calls for 'robust review' of OBR over fears it is holding back growth
union-obr-review-call.body_md:
The Trades Union Congress wants someone to take a hard look at the body that decides how much room the government has to spend money — and it thinks that body has been getting the sums wrong for years.

In a submission ahead of Chancellor John Healey's first Budget on 28 October, the TUC is calling for a "root and branch" review of the Office for Budget Responsibility, the independent watchdog whose forecasts determine whether a chancellor has met the fiscal rules or blown through them. The union's complaint is technical but consequential: it says the OBR's economic models assume that public investment "crowds out" private capital — that is, every pound the state spends on infrastructure or industry is a pound the private sector would otherwise have spent itself. Strip that assumption out, the TUC argues, and the growth case for bolder public spending looks a great deal stronger.

"For too long, the OBR has been a millstone preventing good growth across the country," said Paul Nowak, the TUC's general secretary. "The world has moved on from the self-defeating logic of austerity, but the OBR models still bake in its false assumptions."

![Paul Nowak, general secretary of the Trades Union Congress](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/46/Paul_Nowak_at_the_TUC_%28cropped%29.jpg/500px-Paul_Nowak_at_the_TUC_%28cropped%29.jpg)

## A dispute over a contested idea

Crowding out is not a settled question in economics — it is one of the oldest fault lines in the discipline. The classical case holds that government borrowing pushes up interest rates and squeezes out private investment; Keynesians counter that when an economy has spare capacity, public spending can pull in private activity rather than displace it. Where an economy sits on that spectrum matters enormously for a forecaster whose job is to tell the Treasury exactly how much fiscal headroom it has.

Alongside the review, the TUC wants the National Wealth Fund's mandate widened so it can back projects on investment horizons of up to 15 years, rather than being judged against the OBR's shorter forecast window — the union's argument being that big infrastructure and industrial bets rarely pay off within a five-year forecast period, and the OBR's methodology penalises them for it.

The Treasury's response was polite but unmoved. A spokesperson said fiscal discipline "remained the foundation of economic stability and national security," and that the government intended to meet its fiscal rules with a buffer against uncertainty — a formulation that stopped well short of endorsing a shake-up of the forecaster that underwrites those rules.

The OBR was created in 2010 precisely to take forecasting out of the hands of chancellors, after years of complaints that Treasury-produced forecasts were consistently, conveniently optimistic. Its credibility since then has been a large part of why gilt markets take UK fiscal rules seriously at all — which is also why any successful push to loosen its assumptions cuts both ways. Investors who currently price UK debt on the OBR's caution might not thank a government for a more generous forecaster, particularly with gilt yields already sitting at the top of the G7 range on unrelated fiscal-flexibility jitters. Healey's Budget on 28 October is the next point at which this argument, still confined to submissions and select-committee testimony, meets an actual fiscal event.
